title: The Original Dixieland band in New York; tailgate trombone; Miff Mole and Teagarden
summary: They discuss the ODJB's influence, Larry Shields' clarinet school, tailgate trombone, and Miff telling Ashcraft about Teagarden in 1928.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: Now, this was about seven, eight years after the New Orleans band, the original Lixie Lane Jazz band, had been in New York. Do you recall that anybody ever spoke about them as having introduced elements of jazz that they hadn't known before?

I think that everybody consciously knew that Nicola Rocca had had quite an influence on everything. I have to get back to Lix again because Lix were awful important. Yeah. And particularly in prescribed tunes where they weren't playing the lovely singing type tunes that Bix played. Also, Larry Shields, in his way, was the founder of a whole school of clarinet. And everybody imitated him. In his way, Emile Christian and Danny Edwards were the origin of tailgate trombone as far as any of us knew.
Well, yet, people like Miff had pretty much his own style.

He was, Miff was the only exception and I think everybody thought of Miff as being a genius on it. Yeah. With his completely own style. The funny part of Miff, in 1928 when my wife and I went, my then fiance and I went down to hear the Roger Kahn band, Miff took me aside and told me that there was a guy playing downtown who was playing more cornet on trombone than he'd ever heard in his life. It was Teagarden.
So, to Miff at that point, what Teagarden was playing was just as different as Brad Gowans with the valve trombone would have been.
